sections.report:
**First read:** The eye lands on the bold title "Help for ferry passengers". It then splits between two equal column heads and starts down the left list. It reads as a plain, calm notice for passengers, maybe a web page or a printed sheet at a landing. It feels orderly and utilitarian.

**Job (assumed):** Tell foot passengers and cyclists what to do before boarding, and how to report a problem.

**Walk: The whole piece**
- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this is for? yes
- Do the image and headline make one idea together? yes (there is no image; the title carries it alone)
- Does every element do a job? yes
- One mood and era? yes
- Is the copy finished? yes
- Do repeated elements look the same? yes (bullets for loose tips and numbers for a sequence is right)
- Do colors, shapes and directions carry the mood? yes
- Does each heading name what its section holds? unsure. "If something goes wrong" (660,148) promises help for any problem. The section only holds a way to report a problem after the crossing by writing a note.

The Bash call to open the catalog entries was refused, so I settled the last line from the image and the standard. I answered it no.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds? No.** The right column head "If something goes wrong" (about x 660–925, y 148–172) promises help for any trouble. The three steps under it (y 190–380) only cover filing a complaint: write down the crossing details, describe the problem, leave a note at the quay office or post it. Someone with a problem on the spot (missed the last boat, lost a bag, someone hurt, bike damaged on board) scans for this heading, finds a write-a-letter process, and gets no immediate route: no crew, no phone number, no "tell a crew member now". Nothing says what happens after the note either: whether there's a reply, a refund, or when. The heading over-promises at exactly the moment a reader most needs it to be accurate.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.4.6 says headings must describe their topic or purpose.
   - **Fix:** Either rename the heading to what the section holds ("To report a problem after your crossing") or make the section match the heading. That means a first line for urgent problems ("Tell a crew member straight away") before the reporting steps, and a closing line saying what the passenger can expect back.
   - Defect. Weight: major, because it's the one place the help sheet fails the reader it most needs to serve.

**What's working.**
- **Lists that match their content.** The left column is unordered bullets for tips that stand alone. The right column is numbered because the reporting steps happen in order. The form tells the reader which list is "any order" and which is "do this, then this" without a word of explanation.
- **Plain, specific copy.** Each tip gives the action and the reason in the reader's own world. For example, "because winter sailings run once an hour and the last boat leaves before dusk", or "so that the gangway is kept clear". A stranger can act on every line without filling a gap.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each heading names what its section holds).

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** "Help for ferry passengers" (about x 90–565, y 65–105) looks about 44 px and heavy bold, more than twice the size of the body text. The reader knows at once what the page is and where to start, so keep that gap in size.
- **There are three clean levels, separated mainly by weight.** The two column headings at y ≈ 160 look about 22 px and bold. The list text looks about 18 px and regular. The difference in size is small, but the jump from bold to regular makes the headings obvious at a glance. This follows Dair's point that a contrast has to be obvious in at least one way, and here weight does that job (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8). The page also uses only three sizes, which fits Bringhurst's advice to work from a small, deliberate scale (*Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1). Keep the bold/regular split if the heading size changes.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've finished the arrangement section. **Section.** Arrangement and space applies. It has one wide title and two columns of list text under it, and nothing else.

**Findings**
1. **Lines of text in neighbouring columns do not sit on the same baselines.** The first item in each column shares baselines at about y≈203 and y≈230. After that the columns drift apart. The left column runs 257, 299, 326… and the right runs 271, 298, 339…. The gap between items (about 14 px) isn't a multiple of the 27 px line spacing, so every item break moves the baselines. By the third item, lines in one column are level with the spaces between lines in the other. Readers read each column down, not across, so the harm is small. What the viewer gets is two blocks that look loosely set next to each other instead of one built page. Müller-Brockmann (*Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid") asks for one set line interval that every column keeps to. Fix: make the space between items a whole line or half a line (27 px or 13.5 px), so both columns share one baseline rhythm. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **The weight does not balance.** The title, the 12-line left column (it ends at y≈555) and the start of the reading all sit on the left. The right column is 6 lines and stops at y≈380. That leaves the lower-right area, about x 660–1280 by y 380–800, empty, and the bottom ~30% of the whole frame is empty too. The page leans to the upper left, and the right column looks like an afterthought, not the other half of a pair. Nothing on the light side balances it. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight. Fix: give the right column more weight. One way is a stronger treatment for "If something goes wrong", since it's what a passenger in trouble needs. Another is a contact detail or a box under the steps. Or, if this is a fixed frame, centre the content block vertically in it. On a scrolling web page the empty space at the bottom is just where the page ends, and only the uneven columns remain. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **The space shows the groups.** The gap from the title to the column headings (~45 px) is wider than the gap from each heading to its list (~25 px). That is wider again than the gap between items (~14 px), which is wider than the space between lines inside an item. Each heading clearly belongs to its own list, and each item reads as one unit.
- **One plain grid.** Two equal columns (x≈90–600 and x≈660–1170) with one gutter and the same 28 px text indent in both lists. The halves read as a pair of equal sections: "before" and "if it goes wrong".

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether this is a fixed frame (slide, printed notice) or a scrolling web page. That decides whether the empty bottom third counts against the balance. Also how the two columns reflow on a narrow phone screen, which matters for passengers reading at the landing.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (lines of text in neighbouring columns share baselines; visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The lines in both columns run about 50 to 60 characters, and the line spacing looks like about 1.5. Each item reads in one pass, and the eye finds the start of the next line easily. Keep this column width if the layout changes.
- The bullets and step numbers hang outside the text, and wrapped lines sit under the first word. That gives each column a clean left edge, so the start of each item is easy to spot and the numbered steps are easy to follow.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**First read.** The eye lands on the bold title "Help for ferry passengers" at the top left, then goes to the two column heads and down the left list. It reads as a plain, calm help notice in near-black on white. There's no colour at all.

**Job (assumed).** A help page or notice that tells ferry passengers how to board and how to report a problem.

**Walk: Color**
- Small palette: yes. It uses one neutral range: near-black text (it looks like about #222) on white, and no hue.
- Strong colour kept to a small share: yes. There's no saturated colour.
- Clear range of light and dark that survives grayscale: yes. Dark text on white is close to the highest value contrast possible. The structure comes from size, weight and position, so it holds up in grayscale unchanged.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. Nothing is set by temperature.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. Title, heads, body and markers are the same near-black everywhere.
- No vibrating edges: yes. There are no adjacent strong colours.
- Status colours keep their usual meaning: yes. None are used.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. No meaning is carried by colour. Bullets and numbers mark the list items.
- Dark theme: yes. It's a light page, so this doesn't apply.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is fully neutral.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- Strong value contrast and one ink colour for all the text. The text looks easy to read, and the colour never competes with the information. The page's structure comes from size, weight and the two columns, so it stays readable in grayscale, on a poor print or on an outdoor screen, which suits a notice that people may read at a landing.
- The near-black text (not pure black) on white softens the glare a little without losing contrast.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
